title: Voyager 1 and 2: Journey Into Interstellar Space | Relaxing Space Documentary
description:
Voyager 1 and 2: the long journey into interstellar space is a calm, slow documentary following two small spacecraft launched in 1977 that are still sending messages home from beyond the Sun's bubble. Drift with them past Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune, and out into the dark between the stars.

This is a gentle, sleep-friendly voyage told with real images and real science from NASA missions: the Grand Tour, the Golden Records, the crossing of the heliopause, and the long quiet that lies ahead. Settle in, dim the lights, and let the Voyagers carry you outward.
tags: calm space video to fall asleep
hook_promise: Two spacecraft with less computing power than a modern key fob, launched in 1977, are still whispering back to us from the dark between the stars, carrying a record of Earth meant to outlast humanity.

chapters.title: Two Small Machines in the Dark
chapters.question: How can something built in the 1970s still be talking to us from beyond the Sun's influence?
chapters.reveal: Voyager 1's signal, travelling at the speed of light, takes about a day to reach Earth, and it is still being heard by giant dishes listening for a whisper weaker than a watch battery's output.
beats: Voyager 1 is now the most distant human-made object, over twenty billion kilometres away, with Voyager 2 following on a different path
A quiet look at the two spacecraft: dish antenna, boom with instruments, golden disc on the side
How the Deep Space Network listens, with giant dishes on three continents
Light-travel time as a way to feel distance: the signal that leaves now arrives about a day later
The promise of the journey: from the planets we know to the space no craft had ever entered
A planted curiosity: why was a rare alignment of planets the reason these two were built at all
chapters.text:
In a quiet room in California, a screen shows a thin line of static, and somewhere inside that static is a voice. It is a very faint voice. It comes from a machine that left Earth before most of its operators were born.

Voyager 1 is now the most distant human-made object. It is more than twenty billion kilometres from the Sun. If you could drive there at highway speed, the trip would take longer than the whole history of human writing.

Its twin, Voyager 2, follows on a different path. It is also far beyond the planets, but it travels in another direction, bending away to the south of the plane where the planets orbit. The two craft are not side by side. They are like two travellers who left the same town and took different roads.

So here is the question. How can something built in the nineteen seventies still be talking to us, from beyond the Sun's own bubble?

Picture one of them, as it would look in a bright room on Earth. The most obvious part is a large dish, about three and a half metres across, shaped like a shallow bowl. It always points back toward home. Beside it, a long boom reaches out, carrying instruments that sample the particles and fields around the craft. Another boom holds the cameras, which no longer have anything much to photograph.

And on the side, bolted to the body, is a gold-coloured disc in a metal case. It is a record, meant to be played by someone who does not yet exist. We will come back to it.

The whole machine is small. It weighs less than a family car. It carries no engine to speak of, only tiny thrusters for turning. And it is running on computers with far less memory than a modern phone.

Now think about what it takes to hear it.

The craft transmits with about as much power as a refrigerator light bulb. By the time that signal crosses the gap to Earth, it has spread so thin that almost nothing remains. What arrives is a whisper, weaker than a billionth of a billionth of a watt. A watch battery gives off far more power than that, every second.

To catch it, we use the Deep Space Network. It is a set of enormous dishes placed on three continents. One group sits in California, one near Madrid in Spain, and one near Canberra in Australia. They are spaced about a third of the way around the world from one another. As Earth turns, one of them is always facing the right patch of sky.

The largest dish is seventy metres wide. Its job is to collect a radio whisper over a huge area. It funnels the whisper into receivers chilled to extreme cold, so they add almost no noise of their own. Then computers pick the pattern out of the hiss.

It is a little like hearing a single person whispering in a stadium, from the far side of the city.

And the signal is not fast to arrive.

Radio waves travel at the speed of light. That is quick enough to circle the Earth seven times in a single second. Yet a message from Voyager 1 takes about a day to reach us.

A day.

When engineers send a command today, they must wait about two days to learn whether it worked. 

This is how far these craft have gone. They began their lives at the planets we knew by name, the bright wanderers our ancestors watched for thousands of years. Then they went past them. Now they are in a place that no spacecraft had ever entered, the thin gas between the stars.

Nobody knew, before they flew, what that place would be like. They were sent to find out.

But there is another question, older than the journey itself. Machines like these were not built on a whim, or because someone had a spare rocket. They exist because of a timing. Something about the arrangement of the planets, in one particular decade, made this mission possible. And it will not happen again for a very long time.

What was it about the planets that made these two small machines possible at all?

 Here is the clean version of that paragraph.

When engineers send a command today, they must wait about two days to learn whether it worked. One day for the words to go out. One day for the reply to come back. It is like holding a conversation where each sentence takes a full day to cross the room.

chapters.title: The Alignment That Comes Once in 176 Years
chapters.question: Why were Voyager's planets lined up like stepping stones, and why did the launch window matter so much?
chapters.reveal: A rare arrangement of Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune let each planet's gravity fling a spacecraft onward to the next, cutting the trip to Neptune from about thirty years to twelve.
beats: The 1960s realisation that the outer planets would be favourably placed in the late 1970s, an alignment recurring roughly every 176 years
The idea of a gravity assist: borrowing a sliver of a planet's orbital motion to speed up
The Grand Tour concept and how it was trimmed to a more affordable mission
Launch in the late summer of 1977, with Voyager 2 leaving first and Voyager 1 on a faster path
Why Voyager 1 would overtake Voyager 2 despite launching later
A moment to feel the hand-off: a tiny craft sliding along curved space from world to world
chapters.text:
The planners at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory were bent over a table of numbers, and one of them noticed something odd. The four giant planets, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune, were drifting into a kind of curve. Seen from above, they would soon sit like stepping stones across a pond.

Why would that matter? And why would a spacecraft have to leave on one particular summer, or wait a very long time for another chance?

The year was nineteen sixty-four. A young graduate student named Gary Flandro was studying the orbits of the outer planets. He found that in the late nineteen seventies they would be spread around the Sun in just the right way. A spacecraft could pass from one to the next, almost without pausing.

Then he worked out how often this happens. The answer was roughly once every one hundred and seventy-six years. That is longer than most nations have existed. The last time the planets had stood this way, Thomas Jefferson was president, and the wide American West was still unmapped.

So there was a window. It would open in the late nineteen seventies, and then it would close for nearly two centuries.

But a good arrangement is only half the story. The other half is a trick of motion, called a gravity assist.

Think of a planet as a vast, slow carousel, circling the Sun. A spacecraft that swings close to it falls into its gravity and is bent onto a new path. In that moment, the craft borrows a sliver of the planet's own motion. It leaves faster than it arrived. The planet slows by an amount so small that no instrument could ever notice it.

The craft pays nothing for this. It needs no extra fuel. It only needs to arrive at the right place, at the right time, from the right direction.

Now the alignment made sense. Each planet could throw the spacecraft toward the next one. Jupiter would send it to Saturn. Saturn would send it onward again. A rocket alone could never carry enough fuel to do this.

The first plan was grand. NASA called it the Grand Tour. It would send several spacecraft to visit all four giants, and perhaps even Pluto. But the price was enormous, and the budgets of the early seventies were shrinking. The plan was cut back.

What survived was smaller, and more careful. Two spacecraft would be built to fly past Jupiter and Saturn. Yet engineers quietly designed them to last much longer than that. If all went well, one of them might still be able to reach Uranus and Neptune.

On the twentieth of August, nineteen seventy-seven, Voyager 2 rose from Cape Canaveral on a Titan rocket. Sixteen days later, on the fifth of September, Voyager 1 followed it.

It seems strange that the second spacecraft to leave was named first. The numbers do not mark the order of launch. They mark the order of arrival.

Voyager 1 was set on a faster, shorter path. It would cross the orbit of Mars, pass through the asteroid belt, and reach Jupiter in the spring of nineteen seventy-nine. Voyager 2 took a gentler curve, and arrived months later.

Somewhere out among the asteroids, the later craft slipped ahead of the earlier one. Two machines had left the same planet within a few weeks of each other. Now one was clearly in front.

Then the planets began to do their work.

Picture one of the spacecraft far from home. Its antenna points back toward a blue point it can barely see. Ahead there is only darkness, and a faint bright disc that grows a little each day.

It does not push through the dark. It falls. Jupiter's gravity reaches out across millions of kilometres, and the craft slides along the curve that gravity makes in space. It swings around the planet, picks up speed, and is released toward the next world.

Nothing is fired. Nothing is spent. A small machine is simply handed from one planet to another.

When the plan was finally complete, the arithmetic was clear. A direct flight to Neptune would have taken about thirty years. With the planets in their rare places, Voyager 2 would need only twelve.

That saving was not just convenience. It meant that people who watched the launch could still be alive to see the arrival. But first came the nearest giant, and it was already growing in the cameras, striped and enormous, with something strange waiting on the edge of its moon.

chapters.title: Jupiter: A Storm Larger Than Earth
chapters.question: What did the first close look at Jupiter reveal that no telescope could?
chapters.reveal: Voyager 1 discovered an active volcano on Io, the first time eruptions had ever been seen on another world.
beats: Approach to Jupiter and the first detailed views of the banded clouds
The Great Red Spot seen up close as a swirling storm wider than Earth
Faint rings discovered around Jupiter
Europa's cracked, young-looking ice surface and the first hints of a hidden ocean question, which remains open
The moment a navigation engineer spotted a plume on the edge of Io's disc
What Io's volcanoes told us about tidal heating from Jupiter's gravity
chapters.text:
Nine days before it came close, Jupiter was already larger in the camera than the full Moon appears in our sky. Its clouds ran in long pale and rust-coloured bands, and they were moving.

In the control rooms on Earth, people watched these pictures arrive one slow line at a time. No telescope had ever shown Jupiter like this. From Earth, the planet is a small striped disc, and its finest details blur in our own turbulent air. Now the details were sharpening each day. So what would a close look reveal that no telescope could?

The bands came first. They were not painted stripes but rivers of cloud, running in opposite directions at different latitudes. Where one stream slid past another, the edges curled into small eddies and braids. Some of those eddies were wider than a country. The whole surface looked less like a ball and more like a slow, enormous current.

Then the Great Red Spot rolled into view. Astronomers had watched it for centuries as a dull red smudge. Up close, it was a storm, turning counterclockwise, with clouds curling around its rim. It was wider than Earth. You could have set our whole planet inside it, with room to spare. Around it, smaller white storms were drawn along and stretched into thin ribbons.

Voyager kept falling inward. And when the cameras looked at the dark space beside the planet, they found something faint.

It was a ring.

Jupiter has a ring, thin and dim, made of fine dust. It is nothing like the bright rings of Saturn that we will meet soon. This one is so faint that sunlight passes through it almost unnoticed. It took a spacecraft looking back from the right angle to see it at all.

Then came the moons. Europa looked like a polished egg that had been cracked and mended many times. Its surface was pale ice, laced with long dark lines, and it had almost no craters. That told scientists the surface was young, perhaps only tens of millions of years old. Something was renewing it. One idea was that liquid water lay beneath the ice, warmed from below. Whether that is true is still an open question, and later missions are still working on it.

But the strangest moon was waiting. Io had been a small orange-yellow disc, blotched with red and black, and strangely free of craters. A few days after the closest approach, an engineer named Linda Morabito was checking the pictures to see how well the craft was aiming. She was not looking for science at all. She was looking for stars, so the navigation could be trusted.

She stretched the brightness of one image of Io. At the edge of its disc, beyond the dark limb, a pale fan of light rose into the blackness. It did not belong to any mountain. It looked like a cloud of something rising from the moon.

She checked it again. It was still there.

Her first thought was that it must be another moon, hidden behind Io. The sums did not fit. No moon of that size could sit in that spot. The plume was real, and it rose more than two hundred kilometres above the surface. That is roughly the distance from one city to the next, straight up.

Voyager 1 had found an active volcano on Io. It was the first time eruptions had ever been seen on another world.

Soon more were counted. Several were erupting at once, throwing sulphur and gas high above the ground. This explained why Io had no craters. New lava and fresh deposits were burying them faster than they could form.

But why would a small, cold moon be so hot inside? The answer is Jupiter's gravity. Io does not circle in a perfect circle, and its neighbours tug on it in rhythm. So Jupiter squeezes and relaxes the moon, again and again, every few days. The rock flexes, and the flexing makes heat, the way a paperclip grows warm when you bend it back and forth.

Here was an engine that needed no sunlight. Gravity alone could keep a world alive. And if it worked for Io, it might work for Europa too. Which was exactly the question the mission would carry onward, toward the next giant, and a planet wearing something stranger than clouds.

chapters.title: Saturn and the Mystery of the Rings
chapters.question: Why do Saturn's rings look woven, braided, and strangely complex up close?
chapters.reveal: Voyager showed that the rings are made of thousands of narrow ringlets shaped by tiny moons, and even revealed odd dark spokes that appear and fade across them.
beats: Arriving at the ringed planet and seeing the rings resolve into thousands of ringlets
Shepherd moons that hold ring edges sharp with gentle gravity
The strange radial spokes, still only partly understood
A path past Titan, its thick orange haze hiding its surface
Why Voyager 1 chose Titan and left the plane of the planets for good
What the rings are made of: mostly water ice, from dust grains to house-sized chunks
chapters.text:
Through the camera's narrow eye, Saturn looked wrong, and the engineers knew it at once.

From far away, the rings had seemed like a few smooth bands, flat as a record. But as Voyager 1 closed in, in November of nineteen eighty, the bands began to break apart. Each one split into thinner lines, and each of those split again. Some looked braided. Some looked oddly knotted, as if someone had woven them by hand. Why would a ring of loose ice look so intricate?

Then the picture sharpened further, and the count kept climbing. There were not a handful of rings. There were thousands of narrow ringlets, packed side by side like the grooves on that same record. Each ringlet was a separate lane of orbiting material, and some lanes were only a few kilometres wide.

Something had to be keeping those lanes apart. Ice orbiting a planet should spread out over time, like milk drifting through tea. Yet the edges here were sharp enough to cut.

The clue came from the edge of a thin outer ring, called the F ring. There, Voyager's cameras found two small moons, running just inside and just outside a thin, kinked ribbon of ice. They were each only about a hundred kilometres across. Scientists named them Prometheus and Pandora, and called them shepherd moons.

The idea is simple, and rather gentle. A moon orbiting just inside a ring pulls on stray particles and nudges them back. A moon just outside does the opposite. Neither one touches the ring. Their gravity alone holds the edge in place, the way two patient sheepdogs keep a flock on a path.

Shepherds explained some of the sharp edges. They did not explain everything, and Voyager found something stranger still.

Across the broad middle ring, faint dark wedges appeared, pointing outward like the spokes of a wheel.

They were not fixed in place. Some formed within minutes and stretched for thousands of kilometres. Then they faded, while new ones appeared elsewhere. The leading idea is that tiny charged dust grains briefly lift off the ring, perhaps lofted by electrical storms or by the planet's magnetic field. Scientists still debate the details, and the spokes remain only partly understood.

Meanwhile, the spacecraft had a decision to make. Beyond the rings lay Titan, Saturn's largest moon, larger than the planet Mercury. Telescopes had shown that it wore a thick orange haze, and that it held an atmosphere denser than Earth's. No one could see its surface at all.

Voyager 1's cameras looked at that haze and saw almost nothing. It was a smooth, butterscotch ball, with a faint darker band near the north pole. The surface stayed hidden. But the instruments measured the air as the craft passed behind the moon, and found mostly nitrogen, the same gas that fills most of our own sky, with traces of methane. A cold, strange cousin of an early Earth, perhaps.

That close pass was the reason Voyager 1 would never see another planet. To fly near Titan, the craft had to take a path that bent it northward, away from the plane where the planets travel. That bend flung it up and out of the solar system's flat disc, and it has been climbing away ever since. Voyager 2 could still visit worlds beyond Saturn. Voyager 1 had traded them all for a single hazy moon.

The rings, meanwhile, gave up their makeup. They are made mostly of water ice, with a little dust mixed in. The pieces range from grains as small as smoke to boulders as big as a house. Together, they form a disc hundreds of thousands of kilometres wide, yet in places only about ten metres thick.

If you could stand among them, you would see a slow, glittering drift of snowballs, gliding by in silence.

So the braids and knots were never decoration. They were the fingerprints of tiny moons, and of forces nobody had yet named. And beyond Saturn, the path split in two. One craft was rising away into empty space, and the other was still bound for a pair of planets no one had ever seen up close.

chapters.title: The Photograph From Six Billion Kilometres
chapters.question: What happens when a spacecraft turns around to look at its own home?
chapters.reveal: In 1990 Voyager 1 captured Earth as a pale speck less than a pixel wide, suspended in a beam of scattered sunlight.
beats: After Saturn, Voyager 1 is sent up and out of the planetary plane
The idea of turning cameras back to take a family portrait of the solar system
The 1990 images of the planets, with Earth as a tiny point of light
Why the sunbeam in the picture is an artefact of scattered light in the camera, and happens to be the lens's own glare
What it means to see all of human history on one pixel
A quiet pause to simply look at the image and the dark around it
chapters.text:
The cameras were switched off on purpose, and nobody was sure the last picture would be worth taking.

By then Voyager 1 had left the planets far behind. After Saturn, its path had carried it up and out of the plane where the planets circle. There were no more worlds ahead to photograph. So the cameras had nothing left to do, except one thing.

What happens when a spacecraft turns around to look at its own home?

The idea came from the astronomer Carl Sagan, who had worked on the cameras' planning. He asked whether the craft could look back, once, before the cameras were shut off for good. Some engineers were doubtful. Pointing a sensitive camera so close to the Sun might burn out its detector. And the pictures would show no new science, only a few faint dots on black.

But the request was kept alive, and in the end it was approved. The date was the fourteenth of February, nineteen ninety. Voyager 1 was about six billion kilometres from the Sun. A signal travelling at the speed of light needed more than five hours to cross that distance.

Over several hours, the camera swung from place to place and took sixty frames. It was building a family portrait of the solar system, one patch of sky at a time. Each frame was sent home slowly, at a trickle, across all that dark.

Neptune was in there, and Uranus. Saturn, Jupiter, Venus. Mars was too faint to be found in the glare. Mercury was lost too, too close to the Sun, and tiny Pluto was too dim and far away.

Then came the frame that mattered most.

Earth was there. It was not a disc, and it had no oceans or clouds. It was less than a single pixel wide, a pale blue speck, and nothing more.

Something else stands out in that frame. A thin band of light runs across it, and Earth sits right inside it. It looks almost deliberate, as if the planet were being lit by a single ray from above. But this was not sunlight, shining kindly on us. It was the camera's own trouble. The Sun was so close to the edge of the view that its light scattered inside the lens and the tube, and spread into streaks. Earth simply happened to land within one of them.

So the beam is a flaw, an accident of glass and geometry. And yet it is hard to look at the picture and see anything else. A tiny world, held in a shaft of light, in the middle of a great dark room.

Every person who ever lived is on that pixel. Every king, every farmer, every child who ever learned to walk. Every war, every song, every harvest and every goodbye happened on that small point, less than a thousandth of the picture's width.

That is not a sad thought. It is simply a true one. From this distance, there is no sign of borders, or cities, or voices. There is only a blue speck, and the light that happens to fall across it.

Look at it for a moment. Look at the dark around it, too, which fills almost the whole frame. It is not empty exactly, only quiet and unlit. Out here, the Sun is just the brightest of the stars, and the home we know is something you can lose by blinking.

Soon afterward, the cameras were turned off. They have not been turned on again. Voyager 1 kept going, carrying its instruments, still listening, still sending numbers home.

And somewhere far behind it, its twin was still moving through the planets, with two more worlds ahead that no camera had ever seen.

chapters.title: Voyager 2: Alone at Uranus and Neptune
chapters.question: What did the only spacecraft ever to visit the ice giants find?
chapters.reveal: At Neptune, Voyager 2 found supersonic winds, a Great Dark Spot, and ice volcanoes erupting on Triton, a moon that likely began its life orbiting the Sun.
beats: Voyager 2 continues alone toward worlds no one had seen
Uranus in 1986: a pale, almost featureless blue-green planet tipped on its side, with a strongly tilted magnetic field
Miranda's patchwork of cliffs and canyons
Neptune in 1989: bright clouds and the Great Dark Spot
Triton's retrograde orbit and nitrogen geysers, with its capture from the Kuiper Belt as the leading idea
The fact that no other craft has visited these planets since, an open frontier
chapters.text:
On the twenty-fourth of January, nineteen eighty-six, a small group of engineers watched a blurry image build up on a screen. It showed a pale disc, blue-green, almost without features. Everyone in the room had waited nearly nine years to see it.

Voyager 2 had left Saturn behind and kept going alone. No other craft had ever been sent past Saturn. Ahead lay two planets that, in any telescope, were only faint smudges of colour. What would a single machine find at the very edge of the known planets?

Uranus was the first answer, and it was a quiet one. The planet looked like a smooth ball of pale cyan, with no bands and no great storms. There was hardly a mark on it that the camera could hold on to.

But the planet itself was strange. Uranus lies tipped over on its side, so that it rolls around the Sun like a ball along a track. Its poles take turns facing the Sun, each for about forty-two years of continuous daylight, followed by the same stretch of night.

The magnetic field was stranger still. It was tilted about sixty degrees away from the spin axis, and its centre sat well off from the middle of the planet. Nobody had expected that. Why a world would carry its field so crookedly is still not fully explained.

Then came the smallest of the five large moons, Miranda. Voyager 2 passed very close, and the pictures looked like a patchwork. There were smooth plains beside grooved ridges, and canyons many times deeper than the Grand Canyon. One cliff was about twenty kilometres high, tall enough that a stone dropped from its top would fall for several minutes.

Nobody is certain how a moon only about the width of England could end up so scrambled. One idea says it was broken apart and pulled back together. Another says it was heated and stretched from within.

Voyager 2 flew on. Its radio signal, already weak, grew weaker. Out here the Sun is a hard, small point of light, many hundreds of times dimmer than it appears from Earth. The cameras had to take long exposures to see anything at all, and engineers rotated the whole spacecraft to keep the pictures from smearing.

In August of nineteen eighty-nine, Neptune came into view. After the pale calm of Uranus, it looked like a different kind of world. The blue was deeper, and thin white clouds of frozen methane streaked across it high above the atmosphere. Near the middle of the planet sat a dark oval, about the size of Earth.

It was named the Great Dark Spot. A storm, then, like Jupiter's, in a place where there was hardly any sunlight to drive it.

And the winds were fast.

Around the Great Dark Spot they blew at roughly twelve hundred kilometres an hour. That is close to the speed of sound in our own air. On a world where it was about minus two hundred degrees Celsius, the air was moving faster than anywhere else Voyager had measured.

Some years later, the telescope pictures showed that the Great Dark Spot had vanished. Storms on Neptune, it seems, come and go.

Last of all came Triton, Neptune's largest moon. It circles the planet backward, against the direction Neptune spins. That alone was a clue. A moon that formed beside its planet would almost never do this.

Then the camera showed the surface. It was pink and white, with smooth ice and a texture like the skin of a cantaloupe. And across the southern ice lay dark streaks, all pointing the same way, as if blown by a wind.

They were plumes. Nitrogen gas, mixed with dark dust, was rising several kilometres into the thin air and drifting sideways.

It was snowing upward, on a world at minus two hundred thirty degrees.

The most likely explanation is that Triton did not begin here. It probably started life orbiting the Sun, a member of the Kuiper Belt, the icy region beyond Neptune. Neptune caught it long ago, and the pull of the planet heated and reshaped it. The plumes themselves are probably driven by faint sunlight warming nitrogen ice.

So the only visit to these two planets was a few days each, nearly forty years ago. No other spacecraft has gone back. Everything we know about the ice giants up close comes from one machine passing at high speed.

Voyager 2 had finished with the planets. Neptune fell away behind it, one small blue point among the stars. But the story was far from over, because ahead there was still an edge to find.

chapters.title: The Edge of the Sun's Bubble
chapters.question: Where does the Sun's reach actually end?
chapters.reveal: Voyager 1 crossed the heliopause in 2012 and Voyager 2 in 2018, and both found that the plasma outside is denser than inside, a flat measurement that confirmed they had truly left.
beats: The solar wind as a constant stream flowing outward from the Sun
The termination shock, where the wind abruptly slows
The heliosheath, a turbulent region of compressed, hot plasma
The 2012 crossing, confirmed by plasma waves that revealed rising density
Why the crossing was only recognised after careful analysis, and why Voyager 2's instruments gave a cleaner picture
How the bubble shields the inner solar system from cosmic rays
chapters.text:
Some of the instruments on Voyager 1 have been quietly counting charged particles for nearly half a century. In twenty twelve, the counts began to change in a way nobody had seen before. The particles from the Sun were fading, and particles from somewhere else were rising. So where, exactly, does the Sun's reach end?

To answer that, we have to start with something the Sun is always doing. It is throwing itself away. A thin stream of charged particles, mostly protons and electrons, flows outward in every direction, at about four hundred kilometres each second. This is the solar wind. It is far too thin to feel, thinner than the best vacuum you could make in a laboratory on Earth.

The wind does not stop at the planets. It sweeps past Neptune, still moving, still carrying the Sun's magnetic field with it. Then, far out, it meets resistance. The space between the stars is not empty. It holds its own faint gas, and that gas pushes back.

The first sign of this was the termination shock. Here the wind, which had been travelling faster than sound can move through it, suddenly slows down. Voyager 1 crossed this boundary in two thousand and four. Voyager 2 followed in two thousand and seven.

Past the shock lies a stranger place, called the heliosheath. The particles pile up here, compressed and heated to tens of thousands of degrees. Yet it would not feel hot. The gas is so thin that a spacecraft passing through gains almost no warmth at all. The magnetic field twists and tangles, and the plasma moves in slow, turbulent currents.

For years the two craft drifted through this region, sending back readings every day. Then, in the summer of twenty twelve, the instruments began to disagree with the old picture. The Sun's particles dropped sharply. Cosmic rays, which come from distant exploded stars, climbed higher than ever recorded.

It looked like an exit. But the team did not announce it.

The trouble was that Voyager 1's plasma instrument had stopped working in nineteen eighty. It could not measure the surrounding gas directly. The scientists had to wait, and they were still uncertain. They could only see the particles change, and they could not say for sure what lay on the other side.

Then the Sun gave them a clue. A great burst of material had erupted from its surface months earlier, and it finally reached the spacecraft. The shock wave made the surrounding plasma ring, like a struck bell. The antenna picked up the vibration, and the pitch of that ringing told the team how dense the plasma was.

The density was about forty times higher than inside the heliosheath.

That was the answer. The gas outside the bubble is cooler, but it is far denser than the thin, hot plasma of the Sun's own wind. A flat, simple number, and it settled the matter. Voyager 1 had crossed the edge, the heliopause, in August of twenty twelve, though the proof took more than a year to arrive.

Voyager 2 crossed in November of twenty eighteen. And its plasma instrument still worked. It saw the wind fall away in a single day, and the density jump up on the other side. This was the clean view that Voyager 1 never had. Together, the two craft showed that the boundary is real, and that it is not in the same place everywhere.

This edge matters to us, far more than it first seems. The bubble that the Sun blows around itself acts like a shield. It turns away a large share of the galactic cosmic rays, those fast, energetic particles that can damage living cells and the machines we build. Without it, the radiation reaching the inner planets would be much stronger.

So the small, sheltered world we live on sits inside a protective bubble, one that the Sun has been making for billions of years. And the two craft have now passed through its wall. What waits for them out there is not a void, but a faint, steady sea of gas, and every instrument still running is listening to it.

chapters.title: The Golden Records
chapters.question: What would you say to the universe if you could only send one message?
chapters.reveal: Each Voyager carries a gold-plated copper record, built to last for a billion years, holding greetings in dozens of languages, music, and sounds of Earth.

The instructions etched on the cover showing how to play it
The pulsar map that points back to our Sun's location
The honest fact that the chances of it ever being found are tiny, and that it is mainly a message to ourselves
A thought experiment: who or what might one day hold it
chapters.text:
Inside each Voyager, bolted to the side of the bus, there is a flat square case the colour of old brass. It holds a disc about the size of a dinner plate. The disc has a groove, just like the vinyl records in a living room, and a needle sits beside it in a small holder, ready to play.

Why would a spacecraft carry a record player? And if you could send only one message to the universe, what would you put on it?

In nineteen seventy-seven, a small team was given that question and about six months to answer it. The idea was old and simple. Sailors had always sealed notes in bottles and thrown them into the sea, with no idea who would find them. Voyager was leaving the Solar System anyway. So why not let it carry one?

The team was led by the astronomer Carl Sagan. They chose the pictures first. There are a hundred and fifteen of them, stored as patterns in the groove. You see a mother and child, a city street, a tree, a pair of hands. You see the planets, and a diagram of how our bodies are built.

Then came the sounds. The record holds wind, rain and thunder. It holds surf on a shore, birdsong, a footstep, a heartbeat, and a mother softly greeting her newborn. Somewhere in the grooves, a kiss lasts a few seconds.

There are also greetings in fifty-five languages, from ancient Sumerian to modern Chinese. One of them is only a few words long. It simply says, hello, to the children of the stars, we wish you well.

And there is music, nearly ninety minutes of it. A Peruvian wedding song. A Navajo night chant. Bach, Beethoven, and a blues guitar. Pipes from the Solomon Islands, and drums from Senegal. Every piece is a small proof that people have always tried to say something beautiful to whoever might be listening.

Yet a record is useless without a way to play it. So the cover of each disc carries instructions, etched in the metal. There are no words, because no words could be trusted to be understood. The diagrams show a stylus, a turntable, and the speed at which to spin it. They show how to read the pictures, too, using a circle drawn on the cover as a guide.

A binary mark on the cover gives the time for one turn of the record. It is measured against a basic ticking of the hydrogen atom, something any scientist would know.

Beside those diagrams sits a strange star-like drawing, a set of lines that radiate from one point.

It is a map to us.

Each line points toward a pulsar, a spinning star that flashes at a steady rhythm. The length of each line is written in the pulsar's own period, the pulse count itself. A reader who knows the pulsars could find where all those lines meet. That place is our Sun. Because pulsars slow down at known rates, the map can even hint at the date of launch.

Now for the honest part. The chances of anyone finding this record are tiny. The space between stars is so empty that Voyager will pass no star closely for tens of thousands of years. Even then it will pass at a distance of light-years. A finder would need to be extremely lucky, and very near.

Sagan said as much. He wrote that the record was cast upon the cosmic ocean, and that the launching of such a bottle says something very hopeful about life on this planet. So it is mainly a message to ourselves. It asks what we would choose to say about who we are, if we had to be brief.

The disc itself is built for patience. Each record is copper, coated in gold, and the gold protects it. Out in the cold and the dark, with only the faintest dust to wear it down, it should stay readable for roughly a billion years.

A billion years is longer than any language we speak. It is longer than any country, any city, or any coastline we know. By then the Sun may have changed and the continents may have moved. The record would still be there, quietly turning in the dark, if anyone ever picked it up.

So picture who that might be. A traveller, perhaps, drifting across the dark. They notice a small metal object with an odd shape. They cannot know what a mother is, or what rain is. They may not have hands, or eyes. And yet something in the order of the thing, the careful diagrams and the patient circles, would tell them it was made on purpose.

They might never hear the greetings. But they would know that someone had tried.

And that is the real question the record leaves behind. How long can two small machines keep carrying it, with their power slowly fading?

chapters.title: The Long Quiet Between the Stars
chapters.question: What will Voyager do when its last instrument falls silent?
chapters.reveal: Long after the radios fail, the Voyagers will keep drifting, and in about forty thousand years Voyager 1 will pass within a couple of light-years of a faint star in the constellation Ursa Minor.
beats: The slow shutdown of instruments to save the dwindling power from the plutonium generators
The expected end of communication sometime in the coming years, an honest estimate rather than a date
How empty interstellar space is, and how little will happen to the craft over time
Voyager 1's and Voyager 2's future close approaches to distant stars, measured in tens of thousands of years
The Milky Way orbit: they will circle the galaxy for billions of years
A final calm image of two small points moving together through starlight, carrying a message that outlasts us
chapters.text:
Every few months, an engineer at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory sends a short list of commands to a machine that is more than twenty billion kilometres away. The commands ask it to turn off something it has carried since nineteen seventy-seven. A heater, perhaps, or an instrument that has measured its last magnetic field.

Nobody enjoys sending these commands. But the power has to come from somewhere, and the source is running down.

Each Voyager carries three small generators filled with plutonium. As the plutonium decays, it gives off heat, and the heat becomes electricity. That supply falls by about four watts every year. A watt is a very small thing, less than the glow of a night light. Each one lost means something on board must go quiet.

So the instruments are switched off one at a time. The cameras went long ago. Other sensors have followed, and only a few remain. So here is the question the engineers cannot avoid. What will Voyager do when its last instrument falls silent?

The honest answer about the radio comes first. Nobody can give a date. The team speaks of the coming years, and even that is an estimate, not a promise. A fault could end the signal sooner. Careful planning could stretch it a little longer. One day the last tone will not arrive, and the dishes on Earth will listen to nothing but the faint hiss of the sky.

And then, nothing will change for the spacecraft.

Silence does not stop a Voyager. It was never pushing itself along. Its engines finished their work decades ago, and since then it has simply coasted. The Sun's gravity pulls on it very gently, but it is moving far too fast to be held. Without power, it keeps going exactly as before.

Out there, very little can disturb it. Interstellar space is not truly empty, but it is close. A cubic centimetre, about the size of a sugar cube, holds only a few atoms. On Earth, the air in the same space holds billions of billions. A Voyager could travel for a very long time and meet almost nothing.

There will be slow wear. Cosmic rays will pit the metal a little. Tiny dust grains will strike now and then, though rarely. The record itself is sheltered by its cover from the worst of it. Over millions of years, the edges will soften. But the structure will remain, because in that cold and that quiet, there is almost nothing to take it apart.

So where will the Voyagers go? Not toward anything, exactly. They are not aimed at any star. But they will pass some.

In about forty thousand years, Voyager 1 will drift within a couple of light-years of a faint star in the constellation Ursa Minor, the Little Bear. That is closer than most stars ever come to our Sun. Even so, it is a distance of many trillions of kilometres. The star will look like one bright point among others, and the craft will not slow down to look.

Voyager 2 will make a similar pass near the star Ross 248, also in about forty thousand years. Modern humans have existed for only about three hundred thousand years. Everything we have built, from the first cities to the last message, fits inside a fraction of the wait.

Beyond those meetings, the path simply continues. The Sun moves around the centre of the Milky Way, taking about two hundred and thirty million years to make one circuit. The Voyagers move with the galaxy, on their own orbits, close to our own. They will circle the Milky Way for billions of years. Long after the Sun has changed, and perhaps after Earth has too, they may still be turning.

Think of the picture, then, after the last signal.

Two small points, far apart and yet moving together, passing through the light of other suns.

No sound reaches them. No one watches. Each one holds a disc of gold, with a song, a greeting, and a map back to a star that will have moved on. They do not know what they carry. We did the knowing for them, once, a long time ago.

We sent them out of curiosity, and a little hope. That much has already been done, and nothing can undo it.

So let them go on, quietly, between the stars. The night is wide and slow, and you have travelled a long way tonight. Rest now. Goodnight.

cold_open:
Two spacecraft, built with less computing power than a modern key fob, are still sending messages home from the dark between the stars.

They were launched in nineteen seventy-seven. We thought they would fall silent within a few years. But they kept going, past giant storms, past rings of ice, out beyond the edge of the Sun's own bubble.

How does a signal so faint cross so much emptiness? And why does each machine carry a golden record, a portrait of Earth meant to outlast us?

Soon you will see Jupiter's great storm, the rings of Saturn, and a pale blue dot photographed from six billion kilometres away.

Listen.

There is nothing to do tonight but listen. No hurry, no noise, only real science, told slowly, over the most beautiful pictures these travellers ever sent.

Let us follow the faint voice outward.

shorts.title: The Voice That Takes a Day to Reach Earth
shorts.hook: A whisper from twenty billion kilometres
shorts.narration: A machine built in the nineteen seventies is still talking to us, and its voice is weaker than a billionth of a billionth of a watt. Voyager 1 is more than twenty billion kilometres from the Sun, and it transmits with about as much power as a refrigerator light bulb. By the time that signal reaches Earth, almost nothing is left. A watch battery gives off far more power every second. To catch it, enormous dishes in California, Spain and Australia listen as the planet turns, and chilled receivers pull the pattern out of the hiss. It is like hearing one person whisper in a stadium from the far side of the city. And the message takes a full day to arrive. The full journey of the Voyagers is waiting on the channel.

shorts.title: A Pale Blue Speck Smaller Than a Single Pixel
shorts.hook: Everyone you know is on this pixel
shorts.narration: Everyone who ever lived is inside a single pixel. On the fourteenth of February, nineteen ninety, Voyager 1 turned around from about six billion kilometres away and took one last look at home. Earth was less than one pixel wide, a pale blue speck caught in a streak of scattered sunlight. The beam was only a flaw in the camera lens, yet it looks like a tiny world held in a shaft of light, in the middle of a great dark room. Every king, every farmer, every song and every goodbye happened on that small point. From there, you could lose it by blinking. The full journey of the Voyagers is waiting on the channel.
